lesson.title: Sitting Down to Stand Up: The Sit In Movement
lesson.summary: On February 1, 1960, four Black college students sat down at a whites only lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, and refused to leave, igniting a wave of student led sit ins across the South that pressured hundreds of businesses to desegregate.
lesson.body:
On February 1, 1960, four freshmen from North Carolina Agricultural and Technical College, Ezell Blair Jr., who later took the name Jibreel Khazan, Franklin McCain, Joseph McNeil, and David Richmond, walked into the F. W. Woolworth store in downtown Greensboro, North Carolina, sat down at the lunch counter reserved for white customers, and ordered coffee. They were refused service and asked to leave, but they stayed seated, quietly, until the store closed. They returned the next day, and the day after that, joined by growing numbers of fellow students.

The tactic was not entirely new. Similar sit ins had occurred in a handful of Southern and Northern cities in earlier years, and organizations like the Congress of Racial Equality had experimented with the approach as far back as the 1940s. What made Greensboro different was the speed and scale at which the idea spread. Within days, students in other North Carolina cities staged their own sit ins, and within two months the tactic had reached dozens of cities across the South, involving thousands of students. Nashville, Tennessee, became one of the movement's most disciplined centers, where students including Diane Nash trained in the philosophy and practical tactics of nonviolent resistance through workshops led by James Lawson, a minister who had studied Gandhian nonviolence directly in India.

The tactic itself was simple but demanding: sit peacefully and orderly at a segregated counter, dress neatly, and remain calm and nonviolent no matter what provocation followed, whether verbal abuse, having food or drinks poured on them, physical assault, or arrest. This discipline was deliberate. By refusing to respond in kind, protesters made the hostility of segregationist bystanders and, often, local police, visible to a national audience following the story in newspapers and on television, turning public sympathy against the system defending the lunch counters rather than against the students challenging it.

The economic pressure worked. Store owners depended on general customers, and boycotts combined with the sit ins' disruption of business cut into revenue significantly. By the summer of 1960, many chain stores, including the Greensboro Woolworth's where it had all started, agreed to desegregate their lunch counters. Just as importantly, the sit in movement demonstrated the organizing power and moral seriousness of a new generation of student activists, energy that Ella Baker channeled that same spring into founding the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, giving the movement's youngest and most energetic wing a permanent organizational home.
